claims.text: The target material is an as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi high-entropy alloy in nanoscale thin-film or patterned-nanoribbon form.
The unmodified film–substrate interface provides inefficient heat transfer.
Inefficient interfacial heat transfer creates localized thermal gradients during magnetic cycling.
Localized thermal gradients disrupt the intrinsic magnetic phase transition of nanoscale FeMnNiGeSi.

The cited magnetic high-entropy-oxide thin-film evidence supports the general possibility of static magnetic ordering in a high-entropy thin film, but not thermal-gradient disruption of a transition in FeMnNiGeSi.
Localized thermal gradients diminish the magnetocaloric entropy change of nanoscale FeMnNiGeSi.
Localized thermal gradients enhance magnetic hysteresis under low-field cycling.
Adding a thin copper or diamond-like-carbon underlayer will improve thermal connectivity and heat dissipation at the film–substrate interface.
The underlayer will improve interface quality and limit interfacial disorder capable of altering the magnetic phase transition.
Improved thermal connectivity will reduce local temperature gradients.
Reducing local temperature gradients will reduce extrinsic hysteretic losses.
Reducing local temperature gradients will increase the measured magnetocaloric entropy change and cooling capacity.
Underlayer-modified samples will have a significantly smaller hysteresis-loop area than otherwise identical as-deposited controls.
Underlayer-modified samples will have a measurably larger magnetocaloric entropy change than otherwise identical as-deposited controls.
The modified samples will move toward bulk-like magnetocaloric behavior.
The proposed operating range is applied magnetic fields below 100 mT and cycling frequencies below 1 Hz.
Interface-controlled heat transfer is critical in the stated nanoscale geometry and operating range.
The magnitude of improvement may depend on underlayer thickness, uniformity, and interface quality.
